name: parcel-number-generator
oneLiner: Three warehousing services built directly against the architectural constitution — and not one of them is deployed anywhere.
summary: The PNG system issues parcel tracking numbers from a finite pool: never the same number twice, honouring sub-ranges withheld from allocation, without leaking daily volume. Alongside it, a service records events raised against parcels and the warehouse, and an operator console sits over both. It is the most interesting case in the portfolio from a methodological point of view: the repository grew out of a 2018 .NET Framework 4.5.2 solution modernised directly against `architecture-standards`, then absorbed the notification service from a separate `komunikaty` repository (itself modernised from a 2019 WinForms application). The consolidation is documented in ADR-0004 — one of the very few places in the whole portfolio where the 'merge two repositories' pattern was actually carried out rather than merely proposed. The gates are real: CI fails a pull request whose model has drifted from its committed migrations, for both services and both database providers, builds three images and runs them under `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production` to check that the startup guards still refuse to boot without a connection string and without a token issuer.
tests: Two test projects, 112 `[Fact]`/`[Theory]` attributes (the README cites 139 cases — theories expand to more than one apiece). They cover pool arithmetic and the allocation strategies, the API surface of both services, mapping, and the purity of the shared kernel. A separate class enforces that no HTTP route reaches where it should not.
ci: Six workflows: `ci.yml` (tests, `dotnet format`, migration-drift checks for both services and both providers, the architecture guards, three image builds with startup-guard smoke tests, gitleaks over full history, a transitive vulnerability audit), `codeql.yml`, `secret-scan.yml`, and three Fly.io workflows. Warnings are errors, NuGet advisories included.

components.name: Pool domain and allocation strategies
components.description: Pool arithmetic with exclusions and three strategies behind one interface. No package references at all — a fourth strategy is one class and one registration line.

components.name: The notification service
components.description: Transferred here from the deprecated `komunikaty` repository. It normalizes every parcel-number dialect at the edge and stores the canonical form; acknowledgement is idempotent, and the first timestamp wins.

components.name: Operator console and BFF
components.description: The system's only public face. The browser talks to this origin and no other, and the BFF proxies to both services — pool dashboard, batch allocation, dialect-tolerant lookup, the notification board.

components.name: The shared kernel
components.description: Plumbing only, with an 800-line ceiling enforced by a script in CI rather than by prose. Exactly the same pattern as in `architecture-standards-init-example`.

components.name: Per-provider migrations
components.description: A separate migration set per provider, for both services. The drift gate in CI compares the model against the committed set — a schema change without a migration does not pass.

components.name: The deviations register
components.description: The repository's own register of what it does not yet satisfy: what, against which principle, since when, and what closes it. The roadmap is finished when the *Open* table is empty.

overlaps.reason: Built directly against that constitution and measured by it in `02-GAP-ANALYSIS.md`. The deviations register exists here because §3a of that document requires it.
DEV-2 is waiting on a decision about which identity issuer is trusted. `authservice` is the obvious candidate — both services already validate tokens against a JWKS and hold no key material.

The same shape: a shared kernel with a line ceiling, an in-memory database fallback, migrations from a hosted service that starts after Kestrel. Greenfield there, modernization here — the same rules produce the same skeleton from two different starting points.

product: A proof of method, not a transaction. The commercial value is not in issuing parcel numbers — it is in the documented path from a 2018 .NET Framework 4.5.2 solution to three .NET 10 services with migration gates, startup guards and a full-history secret audit. That is precisely the work a modernization consultant is paid for, and here it is shown end to end, including the parts that did not land.
highlights: A consolidation actually carried out: the notification service moved in from a separate repository, with an ADR recording what was harmonized. In a portfolio full of merge proposals, this is one of the few that happened.

The status code carries what the caller should do next: 201 with `complete: false` for a partial batch, 409 when the pool is exhausted and retrying will never help, 503 under contention with `Retry-After`. The difference between 'impossible' and 'try shortly' lives in the protocol, not in the documentation.

A fresh clone runs with no credential at all — an in-memory database fallback — but in Production the startup guard refuses to boot without a connection string and an issuer. CI runs the built images under `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production` for the express purpose of checking that the guards still fire.

The secret audit covers full history, not just HEAD, and is written up as a four-step release procedure of which two steps cannot be performed by a commit. This is the lesson that was missing in `quorum`.
gaps: **Nothing is deployed.** DEV-1: the workflow can stand up the whole estate from a single tag, but no Fly app exists, there is no `FLY_API_TOKEN`, and no migration has touched a real database. Every deployment claim is argued, not measured.
DEV-2: no identity provider is configured. A deployment would be open were it not for the guards — which means the JWKS validation path has never been exercised against a real issuer.
DEV-7: the open-source release is unfinished. The repository has been public since 2026-09-01, but the description and topics (#20) and the GHCR packages (#29) remain outstanding.
Six open Dependabot pull requests out of thirteen open items. Phase 2 of the roadmap exists precisely to clear them, and it has not started.

The 'never the same number twice' guarantee is today proven against an in-memory database. Phase 3 of the roadmap turns it into a measurement against a real engine — until that runs, the system's strongest claim is tested in the weakest place.
next: Close phase 1 of the roadmap: the repository description and topics, a badge row that matches reality, a rendered documentation page. These are minutes of work and they unblock legibility for anyone from outside.
Merge the six Dependabot pull requests in one pass — CI is strong enough to make that safe, and every week of delay raises the cost.
Point `Jwt__Authority` at `authservice` (DEV-2). It needs no code change — the wiring is conditional and already in place — and it unblocks the first deployment.
Push the first `v*` tag and replace the text of DEV-1 with what the first deployment actually measured.
Move the uniqueness proof onto a real database engine under concurrency — it is the one claim in this repository that must not be left resting on an in-memory database.
risks: The entire deployment path is untested in practice: the health-check grace period, the `.flycast` wake path and JWKS validation have never once run. The image builds and smoke tests in CI bound the 'works on my machine' class but not the platform class.
The repository has been public since 2026-09-01 with the release unfinished. A public commit is public forever, and re-privating does not reach the clones and forks that already exist.
headline: Three services, six workflows, a full history audit — and zero deployed environments
